prev: Isomers share a molecular formula. Constitutional (structural) isomers have their atoms joined in a different order. Stereoisomers have the same connections but a different arrangement in space: enantiomers, diastereomers, E/Z isomers. Conformers differ only by rotation about single bonds and interconvert rapidly at room temperature, so they aren’t separate compounds.

name: Cambridge A Level
lede: 36 units covering atomic structure, orbitals and bonding, and all of the organic chemistry in Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry, for exams in 2025 to 2027. Each unit has the syllabus points, lessons, an exam-style question with worked answers, and a quiz.
note: How this course fits the syllabus.

Units 1–6 cover AS topics 1–3 (atomic structure, electrons in orbitals, ionisation energies, bonding, shapes and intermolecular forces). Units 7–22 cover every organic topic: AS 13–22 and A Level 29–37. Units 23–36 cover the physical and inorganic topics (AS 2 and 4–12, A Level 23–28) as lessons with a worked exam-style question; their practice questions are coming in a later update. Each unit shows its syllabus references, and lessons that are only in the A Level part say so. A unit counts as complete when you have mastered 80% of its questions.

prev: Almost all the mass of an atom is in a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons. The electrons occupy the rest of the space, in shells around it. An atom is mostly empty space.

The proton number (atomic number, Z) is the number of protons. The nucleon number (mass number, A) is protons plus neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons; an ion has lost electrons (positive) or gained them (negative).

prev: Electrons occupy shells (principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3 …). Each shell is split into sub-shells (s, p, d, f), and each sub-shell is made of orbitals. An orbital is a region of space that holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins.
Shapes: an s orbital is spherical. A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, with two lobes either side of the nucleus; the three p orbitals (px, py, pz) point along three axes at right angles.

prev: Almost all the mass of an atom is in a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons. The electrons occupy the rest of the space, in shells around it. An atom is mostly empty space.

The proton number (atomic number, Z) is the number of protons. The nucleon number (mass number, A) is protons plus neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons; an ion has lost electrons (positive) or gained them (negative).

prev: Electrons occupy shells (principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3 …). Each shell is split into sub-shells (s, p, d, f), and each sub-shell is made of orbitals. An orbital is a region of space that holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins.
Shapes: an s orbital is spherical. A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, with two lobes either side of the nucleus; the three p orbitals (px, py, pz) point along three axes at right angles.
